lead: A haptic display feels real only if the computer keeps up with your hand. Haptic rendering is a control loop: read hand position, compute force, drive motors, repeat hundreds or thousands of times a second. Split the loop across two arms and you get teleoperation. The hand is fast and stiff and notices a few milliseconds of delay. Uses: surgical trainers, simulators, remote robot arms. Only a few universities teach this chapter.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.6, Chapter 3.7, and basic feedback and stability.

items: Read handle position x from the encoders, in metres.
Collision: find the nearest point on the surface outside the wall, the proxy point x_wall.
Compute the force with the spring-damper law.
Send the force, as motor current, to the actuators.
Repeat next tick. A typical rate is 1 kHz, so T = 1 ms.

blocks.where: F is force in newtons; k is wall stiffness in N/m; x_wall is wall surface position in metres; x is handle position in metres; b is damping in N·s/m; v is handle velocity in m/s. The first term pushes the hand out of the wall; the second brakes it.

blocks.text: The hand is stiff and fast. Fingertip contact stiffness is tens of thousands of newtons per metre. A slow loop delivers force late: the wall feels spongy or the loop buzzes. Haptics runs on its own thread at 1 kHz; graphics draws at 60 to 90 Hz.

blocks.where: b is damping in N·s/m; k is wall stiffness in N/m; T is loop period in seconds. This is a rule of thumb for a virtual wall, not a proof.

blocks.text: With k = 2000 N/m and T = 1 ms, b must exceed 1 N·s/m. With T = 10 ms, b must exceed 10 N·s/m. Ten times the damping feels like thick treacle.
When you cannot raise the loop rate, smooth instead: interpolate force between ticks, filter the force signal, or lower k. A softer stable wall beats a stiff wall that buzzes.

A master arm sits with the operator; a slave arm sits at the remote site. Both carry encoders and motors. The master sends position to the slave controller; the slave sends back position or measured force.

Two common architectures. In position-position, master position commands the slave, and slave position is turned into a master force through a virtual spring. In position-force (master sends position, slave returns force), also called force reflection, the slave returns its measured contact force directly. Position-position is more robust when the slave is stiff; position-force feels contact sooner.

blocks.where: F_master is the force the operator feels in newtons; F_slave is the slave's measured contact force in newtons; α is the force scale factor, a plain number. Use α < 1 when the slave is strong, as with a large industrial arm. Use α > 1 when the slave is weak, as with a tiny surgical tool, so its small forces are magnified for the operator to feel.

blocks.text: Skipping force scaling is a common mistake: the felt force is too large to control or too small to notice. Delay also breaks the loop; even 50 ms causes oscillation, and time-domain passivity is one standard fix. The display is the plant, the computer is the controller, and your hand closes the loop.

figure.caption: The loop closes through the hand: motors make a force, the hand feels it and moves, and the next cycle reads the new position. Force is computed before it is applied, so a slow cycle is felt as delay.

spec.aria: A closed rendering loop that reads hand position, checks collision, computes a spring force, drives the motors, and returns to reading position on the next cycle.

examples.question: A virtual wall has stiffness k = 2000 N/m. Using b > kT/2, find the minimum damping b for T = 1 ms and T = 10 ms, and say what the user feels.
steps: Write the rule: b > kT/2, with k in N/m, T in seconds, b in N·s/m.
The slower loop needs 10 times more damping, so the wall feels thick and treacly instead of crisp. This is why haptics runs at 1 kHz while graphics runs at 60 to 90 Hz.
examples.answer: The damping must exceed 1 N·s/m at 1 kHz and 10 N·s/m at 100 Hz.

traps: Thinking a stiffer virtual wall is always better. With a slow loop, more stiffness means buzzing; fix it with a faster loop or more damping, not a bigger k.
Using T in milliseconds in b > kT/2. T must be in seconds: 1 ms is 0.001, not 1.
Forgetting force scaling in teleoperation, so the operator feels a force the master arm cannot safely deliver.
Confusing the 1 kHz haptic loop with the 60 to 90 Hz graphics frame rate; they are separate threads.
A sign slip in F = k(x_wall − x): the force must push the hand away from the wall, not pull it in.

quiz.q: List the steps of one haptic rendering cycle.
quiz.a: Read position, find the proxy or collision point, compute the force, send it to the motors, repeat.

quiz.q: State the stability rule of thumb for a virtual wall.
quiz.a: b > kT/2, with b in N·s/m, k in N/m and T in seconds.

quiz.q: Why does haptics run at 1 kHz when graphics runs at 60 to 90 Hz?
quiz.a: The hand is stiff and fast, so a slow loop adds delay and the wall feels spongy or buzzes.

quiz.q: A wall has k = 4000 N/m and the loop period is 2 ms. Find the minimum damping.
A teleoperation setup with 50 ms delay oscillates. Give two causes and a fix.
quiz.a: Delay in the loop and too high a master gain or stiffness. Fix by lowering the gain, adding damping, or using time-domain passivity.

quiz.q: What is force scaling and why is it needed?
quiz.a: F_master = α F_slave. The slave may be far stronger or weaker than the master, so scaling keeps the felt force useful and stable.

beyond: Not for the exam. Haptic SDKs such as OpenHaptics and CHAI3D run the loop on a dedicated real-time thread. Research moves toward energy-bounding passivity controllers and data-driven friction models, because a spring-damper cannot reproduce stick-slip. Teleoperation over 5G is active work, where the delay budget decides who leads. Search 'time-domain passivity control', 'haptic texture rendering' and 'bilateral teleoperation architecture'.
